text: 1. Make a joyful noise. See on Ps. 98:6.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 2. Honour. Heb. kabod, also meaning “glory,” and appropriately so rendered here (see Ps. 62:7; 72:19).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Name. See on Ps. 5:11; 7:17.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 3. Terrible. God’s deliverances of the persecuted are terrible to the persecutors (see on Ps. 65:5; cf. Rev. 15:3).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Submit themselves. Heb. kachash, “to feign obedience,” “to cringe” (see Ps. 18:44). The submission referred to here is hollow, insincere, feigned; induced only by the show of God’s power. True submission of heart is induced by the revelation of God’s love.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 4. All the earth. See on Ps. 22:27.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Selah. See on p. 629.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 5. Come and see. See on Ps. 46:8.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 6. He turned the sea. A reference to the crossing of the Red Sea (see Ex. 14:21, 22; Ex. 15:1–21).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Through the flood. A reference to the crossing of the Jordan (see Joshua 3:14–17). With poetic license the psalmist unites this epic episode with that of the Red Sea crossing in one grand picture of God’s interposition for Israel.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Did we rejoice. The joy of the Hebrews was expressed in song (see Ex. 15:1–21).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
7. Behold. God is continually keeping watch to see how the nations behave (see on Ps. 11:4; see PK 535, 536). He is jealous for His people, and will not permit them to be crushed by the enemy.
  “… Behind the dim unknownStandeth God within the shadow,keeping watch above his own.”
  JAMES RUSSELL LOWELL,“The Present Crisis.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: The rebellious. Those who are impatient under God’s restraint, or who defy God. These should not be lifted up with pride, for they must eventually submit to God’s power.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
8. Ye people. Or, “O ye peoples”; the Hebrew is plural, evidently referring to the nations.
Verses 8–12 constitute the third stanza, the heart of the psalm, in which the people are invited to praise God for deliverance before uniting with the psalmist in the act of sacrifice (vs. 13–15).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 9. Our soul. Here used idiomatically for “us” (see on Ps. 16:10). God’s people had been preserved alive despite the danger suffered (see Ps. 3:2; 7:2).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: To be moved. See Ps. 121:3; Prov. 3:23, 26.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 10. Hast proved. God had allowed calamity to come upon Israel as a test of her loyalty to Him.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: As silver is tried. See Zech. 13:9; 1 Peter 1:6, 7; cf. Ps. 12:6. Anciently the refining of silver was a slow process. Israel had suffered long.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 11. Into the net. As wild animals are trapped in a snare (see Hosea 7:12).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Affliction. God never allows His people to be tried beyond their strength (see 1 Cor. 10:13). This verse may allude to the affliction of bondage in Egypt.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 12. Men. Heb. ’enosh, “man in his frailty” (see on Ps. 8:4; 9:19).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Ride over our heads. A figure, perhaps derived from the ancient custom of Oriental conquerors victoriously riding over the bodies of the conquered.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Through fire and through water. This phrase, now part and parcel of the English language, is a graphic representation of the many dangers to which men are exposed.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Wealthy place. Heb. rewayah, “abundance [of drink].” Rewayah occurs elsewhere only in Ps. 23:5, where it is translated “runneth over” (literally, “an overflowing”). Perhaps the idea of “abundance” is intended, and the psalmist is asserting that God has brought the Israelites into a state of abundance. The LXX has anapsuche, as if from the Heb. rewachah, meaning “relief,” “respite.” If rewachah is the correct reading, then there is perhaps an allusion to the relief experienced when the children of Israel reached the Promised Land.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
13. Burnt offerings. See Vol. I, pp. 698–700; cf. Isa. 1:11.
Verses 13–15 form the fourth stanza. The change of pronouns here illustrated is common in Hebrew literature.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Vows. The promises that David had made (see on Ps. 22:25; Ps. 50:14). The Mosaic law had regulations concerning various kinds of vows (see Lev. 27:1–8; see on Lev. 27:9–30; Num. 6:2–21).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 14. Have uttered. The lips opened under the influence of deep emotion.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: In trouble. Especially in times of trouble men are prone to make promise to God (see Judges 11:30, 31; 1 Sam. 1:11). How careful they should be to keep these promises! How often they forget them, when health and prosperity return.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 15. Burnt sacrifices of fatlings. That is, of fatted animals suitable for sacrifice.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Bullocks with goats. Both were required in the worship prescribed by Moses (on the use of these animals in sacrifices, see Vol. I, pp. 698–703).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
16. All ye that fear God. David was willing to bear witness to God’s goodness before all, whether they were his countrymen or not (see on 2 Sam. 15:18).
Verses 16–19 are the fifth stanza. David calls on all faithful worshipers of God to recognize with him that God answers the prayers of those who are sincere and honest.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: I will declare. David speaks for himself, and may well have spoken for the people whose king and leader he was.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: My soul. Used idiomatically for “me” (see on Ps. 16:10).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 18. If I regard iniquity. An axiom in Christian experience. In order for prayer to be acceptable to God, it must be coupled with a purpose to forsake all known sin (see Prov. 28:9; Isa. 1:15; 58:3–5; cf. Ps. 34:15; John 9:31; James 4:3; SC 99, 100; PP 584). “When it is in the heart to obey God, when efforts are put forth to this end, Jesus accepts this disposition and effort as man’s best service, and He makes up for the deficiency with His own divine merit” (EGW ST June 16, 1890).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 19. God hath heard. David did not doubt the answer to his prayer; he expressed his assurance of God’s approval (see Ps. 116:1, 2).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 20. Hath not turned away. Our God is a prayer-hearing and a prayer-answering God (see Ps. 65:2; 1T 120, 121).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 1. God be merciful. The thought and language of this verse are an echo of the blessing of the high priest (see Num. 6:24–26). For other phrases similar to expressions found in the Aaronic blessing, see Ps. 4:6; 31:16; 80:3, 7, 19.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Upon us. Literally, “with us.” The phrase is suggestive of intimate fellowship with God.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Selah. See p. 629.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 2. Thy way. The methods and principles of the government of God, in relation not only to Israel but to all the world. God intended that Israel should be the light of the world. How different would have been the history of Israel had she fulfilled her high calling (see DA 577). In Israel’s experience lies a lesson for the remnant church.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Saving health. Heb. yeshu‘ah, usually translated “salvation”; but also rendered “welfare” (Job 30:15); “help” (Ps. 3:2; Ps. 42:5); “deliverance” (Ps. 18:50; 44:4; Isa. 26:18); “helping” (Ps. 22:1); and “health” (Ps. 42:11).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Among all nations. A call to mission service. God has placed upon the church the responsibility of bringing a knowledge of salvation to all nations.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Govern. Heb. nachah, “to lead,” or “to guide.” God is the great Shepherd of all peoples (see Ps. 23:3). Nachah is used of God’s guiding Israel through the wilderness (see Ps. 78:14). As God led Israel, He will lead all peoples who accept Him as their Shepherd.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 5. Let the people. The repetition of the refrain (see on v. 3) emphasizes the psalmist’s expressed desire that all men—not only Israel of the flesh—should praise God for His goodness to them.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
5. Let the people. The repetition of the refrain (see on v. 3) emphasizes the psalmist’s expressed desire that all men—not only Israel of the flesh—should praise God for His goodness to them.
6. Shall the earth yield. Or, “the earth yielded.” The language may be interpreted as referring to the recent harvest in all its abundance. From this brief reference to the harvest some have concluded that the psalm is a harvest thanksgiving.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Our own God. The phrase expresses an intimacy of fellowship with God.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Shall bless. The clause may also be translated as the expression of a wish: “May God, our own God, bless us!”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
7. God shall bless us. The psalm closes with an expression of the same longing for God’s blessing with which it opened. Through Israel all the world was to be blessed. In a knowledge of Israel’s God as the God of all nations the world would share in God’s blessing upon Israel. A full appreciation of this psalm is possible only with deep appreciation of God’s eternal purpose in calling Israel as His chosen people. It is essentially a missionary psalm, and should be precious to the church in its worldwide mission program.
That the psalm was intended for use in public worship seems evident from its reference to the Aaronic blessing, the use of the refrain, and the abundance of words common to public worship, such as “praise” and “bless.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 1. Let God arise. See on Ps. 3:7. Ps. 68 opens with a series of statements similar to the expressions of the formula used “when the ark set forward” in the wilderness (Num. 10:35). Solomon used similar phraseology when the ark was deposited in the Temple (2 Chron. 6:41).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 2. As smoke. The figures in this verse express the utter weakness of the enemies before God’s power (see Ps. 37:20; 97:5; Hosea 13:3; Micah 1:4). The last part of v. 2 and the first part of v. 3 show a degree of similarity to the last verse of Deborah’s song (see Judges 5:31).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 3. Be glad. The call to rejoice is emphasized by threefold repetition. Verse 3 closes the introduction to this joyous song of victory.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 4. Extol. From the Heb. salal, which has the basic meaning, “to lift up,” “to exalt.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: That rideth upon the heavens. The Heb. rokeb ba‘araboth has presented many difficulties of interpretation. The KJV translation “heavens” for ‘araboth is remarkable inasmuch as in every other instance ‘arabah apparently means “desert.” However, in Ugaritic, where ‘arabah is spelled with a p instead of a b, the word means “clouds.” The Ugaritic vowelless term rkb ‘rpt, “rider of the clouds,” is a frequently occurring epithet of Baal. Thus by their rendering “heavens,” the translators of the KJV came remarkably close to what is now believed to be a true definition of the term.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Jah. Heb. Yah, a short form for Yahweh (see Ex. 6:3; Vol. I, pp. 171–173; see on Ex. 15:2). This is the only occurrence of the English short form “Jah” in the KJV.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
5. A father. God reveals His character to men by His deeds of beneficence. The more intimately men associate with Him, the more keenly they become aware of His gracious care for His children. Christ “pitched His tent by the side of the tents of men, that He might dwell among us, and make us familiar with His divine character and life” (DA 23).
The phrase “a father of orphans and judge of widows” appears twice in Ugaritic texts describing an ancient righteous king.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 6. God setteth the solitary. The picture may be that of a poor bachelor who has no money to pay for a bride (cf. Jacob; Gen. 29:18) and so could not marry. God cares for him and helps him to found a family. The figure finds a parallel in Ugaritic, where the statement appears, “the house of the unmarried is closed.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Chains. Heb. kosharoth, a word occurring only here in the OT. The KJV translation “chains” is questionable. Recent commentators suggest the meaning “happiness,” or “prosperity.” In Ugaritic the word means “female singers,” so that the phrase may be translated, “leads out prisoners under [the accompaniment of] singers.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 7. When thou wentest forth. This verse introduces the glorious theme of the psalm. Here begins a galaxy of allusions to the triumphal march of Israel through the wilderness to Canaan, God ever leading the way. The historic retrospect extends through v. 18.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Selah. See p. 629.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 8. Dropped. Usually taken from the Heb. nataph, “to drop,” “to drip.” However, it is probably derived from ṭapap, “to toss,” Arabic ṭaffa, “to flap the wings,” and Aramaic ṭpṭp, “to flicker.” In this way a perfect parallel to the first line is obtained. “The earth shook, the heavens tossed.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
Even Sinai. Although God’s presence was continually manifested during the long wilderness journey, His glorious majesty was especially shown at Sinai (see Ex. 19:16–18; PP 339, 340).
The Heb. zeh Sinay, usually rendered “this Sinai,” has been recognized by H. Grimme as an old title of Jehovah, and can be translated “the One of Sinai.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 9. A plentiful rain. Perhaps an allusion to the manna, which God is said to have “rained down” (Ps. 78:24).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 10. Congregation. Heb. chayyah, “flock.” God is Israel’s tender Shepherd (see on Ps. 23:1).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Poor. Descriptive of God’s flock during the time they wandered in the desert, wholly dependent on God.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 11. Gave the word. Verses 11–14 allude to the conquest of Canaan.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Those that published. Heb. mebaśśeroth, “announcers,” from the verb baśar, “to announce.” The form is feminine plural, and hence refers to women announcers. In the setting of the psalm the mebaśśeroth were probably groups or companies of women singers such as celebrated great events, for example, the return of victorious armies (see 1 Sam. 18:6, 7, see on Ex. 15:20, 21).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

12. Kings. Canaanitish kings (see Joshua 24:11–13).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Did flee apace. Or, “they flee, they flee!” a forceful, intensive repetition. When confronted by the might of Israel’s God, earthly kings quickly scatter.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

Did flee apace. Or, “they flee, they flee!” a forceful, intensive repetition. When confronted by the might of Israel’s God, earthly kings quickly scatter.
13. Lien among the pots. This difficult passage has been made clear by Ugaritic (see p. 618). The Heb. shephattayim, translated “pots” in the KJV and “sheepfolds” in the RSV, actually means hearthstones. Ancient homes contained two hearthstones, as do also the homes of many nomad Arabs today. Furthermore, the passage should be translated as a question and connected with the previous verse, “Will ye remain seated by the hearthstones?” The query puts to shame those who, in times of a national emergency, stay at home when great issues are at stake.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Covered with silver. A beautiful image, suggesting the play of sunlight upon the plumage of a dove in flight. Several words and phrases used here find close parallels in Ugaritic. However, the purpose of the picture of this flying dove in the context of this psalm is obscure.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 14. Scattered kings. Evidently a reference to the discomfiture of the kings of Canaan when Joshua invaded the land (Joshua 10:10, 11).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Snow in Salmon. God scattered kings as the snow disappears from Mt. Zalmon. A Mt. Zalmon, a hill near Shechem, is mentioned in Judges 9:48. This hill almost never has snow, being only about 3,000 ft. high. More likely the “Salmon” here is Jebel Haurƒn, east of the Sea of Galilee, the Asalmanos of Ptolemy. Its peaks of 6,000 ft. are snow covered nearly every winter.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 15. Hill of God. Heb. har–’Elohim, literally, “mountain of God,” idiomatically, “mighty mountain” (see RSV).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Hill of Bashan. Bashan was a high plateau region east of the Sea of Chinnereth (see Palestine during the Period of the Judges).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 16. Why leap ye? Rather, “Why look you with envy?” (RSV). The lofty ranges are described as being envious of the hills of Jerusalem. God honored Zion by choosing to place His Temple there (see Ps. 132:13–16).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 17. Twenty thousand. This expression may also be rendered “myriads.” The thought is that the
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Angels. Heb. shin’an, here conjecturally rendered “angels.” Most commentators consider shin’an to be derived from the root shanah, “to repeat,” and thus to mean “repetitions.” The word appears in Ugaritic as tnn, “warrior,” and should probably be so translated here. The reference would then be to the warriors of God, the angelic host, as in the KJV.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: As in Sinai. God Himself, attended by the heavenly hosts, carrying with Him all the majesty and glory that were displayed at Sinai, is now established in Mt. Zion. What a glorious conclusion to the historic retrospect!
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 18. Thou hast ascended. The psalmist employs the figure of a conquering monarch returning victoriously, with a multitude of captives, to describe the heavenly King going up to Jerusalem. There may be here a special reference to the bringing up of the ark (2 Sam. 6:17). Paul picks up the figure of the psalmist and applies it to the ascension of Christ (Eph. 4:8).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Gifts for men. Rather, “gifts among men.” Receiving on God’s part implies giving; He gives in order to receive. “Through the beloved Son, the Father’s life flows out to all; through the Son it returns, in praise and joyous service, a tide of love, to the great Source of all” (DA 21).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
Lord God. Heb. Yah ’Elohim (see on v. 4).
The description of the triumphal procession is here interrupted with an ascription of praise, and the description is not resumed till v. 24.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 19. Loadeth us. The Hebrew verb suggests “carrying like a shepherd,” or “bearing a burden” (see Zech. 12:3).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 20. Issues. Literally, “outgoings,” or “escapes.” The word for “salvation” is literally, “salvations,” emphasizing the multitude of specific instances of salvation, rather than the mere abstract idea.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 21. Hairy scalp. The top of the head, a vital part of the body. Death is the inevitable penalty for sin that is willfully indulged in.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 22. I will bring again. God will find the wicked wherever they may try to hide, and will punish them (see Amos 9:1–3). Note that the words “my people” are supplied. The reference is evidently not to God’s people but to the sinners mentioned in v. 21.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Bashan. See on v. 15.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 23. Dipped in the blood. A figure describing the destruction of the foes (see on Ps. 58:10).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Dogs. See on 1 Kings 21:23.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 24. They have seen. The picture of the triumphal march is resumed.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 25. Timbrels. Possibly a type of drum (see p. 30).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 26. Bless ye God. This verse is probably the song sung by the women mentioned in v. 25.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 27. Little. Heb. ṣa‘ir, meaning also “young,” or “low.” The adjective refers to the ruler of
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
Benjamin, probably Saul. The passage should be rendered, “There is Benjamin, the least rules them.”
Benjamin. Four tribes are mentioned in this verse. Mt. Zion was on the border between Benjamin and Judah. Zebulun and Naphtali may have been used to represent the tribes at the extreme distance from Mt. Zion (see Palestine during the Period of the Judges; cf. Judges 5:18).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Their council. Heb. rigmah. The word is obscure. Commentators explain it to mean “crowd of people,” “cry,” or “noise of weapons.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 28. Commanded thy strength. The psalmist appears to entreat God to make full display of His power, and even to make that display still more impressive in the contingencies ahead.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 29. Thy temple. Heb. hekal (see on Ps. 65:4).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 30. Rebuke. See Ps. 9:5.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Company of spearmen. Rather “wild beast of the reeds,” perhaps used symbolically of Egypt, a leading world power at that time.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 31. Princes. Heb. chashemannim, a loan word from the Egyptian ḥsmn, meaning “natron,” “copper,” or “bronze.” Natron was a famous article of export from Egypt and copper was imported to the Nile country. It is possible that natron, a detergent commonly used in place of soap in ancient times when soap was still unknown, is here designated.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Egypt; Ethiopia. These countries are named as examples of powerful and wealthy nations that will finally seek after God. On the application of this verse to “the beneficent designs of Jehovah for the salvation of the heathen” see PK 370, 371.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 32. Sing unto God. The psalm closes with an invitation to all nations to praise the Supreme God who has so gloriously manifested His power and goodness in leading Israel on its triumphal march from Egypt to Mt. Zion. When Christ ascended to His Father, the angels received Him into the heavenly courts singing in triumph the words of vs. 32–34 (see AA 32, 33). Compare also the similar use made of Ps. 24:7–10. See comment there.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 33. The heavens of heavens. See on v. 4; Deut. 10:14; see also Deut. 33:26.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Voice. See on Ps. 29:3.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 34. In the clouds. God’s majesty and power are especially shown in the dramatic phenomena of the heavens: thunder, lightning, storm.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 35. Thy holy places. From His dwelling place God performs mighty acts which inspire awe, and sometimes fear, in the hearts of all men.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Strength. God’s strength is given to His people (see Ps. 29:11; Isa. 40:29). What a blessed thought: to His own children God imparts His strength and thus makes them equal to every situation that may arise (see Matt. 28:18–20).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Power. Literally, “powers.” On the force of the plural see on v. 20.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Blessed be God. The contemplation of God’s character as depicted in this poem elicits this tribute of praise from the heart of every grateful child of God (see Ps. 66:20).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 1. Save me. Verse 1 strikes the keynote of the psalm.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Waters. Typical of great distress (see on Ps. 32:6; 42:7).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: My soul. Used idiomatically for “me” (see on Ps. 16:10).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 2. Deep mire. See on Ps. 40:2.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: No standing. That is, “no ground to stand on.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Floods. Heb. shibboleth, “a flowing stream,” translated “channel” in Isa. 27:12. Shibboleth is the word that the Ephraimites were unable to pronounce when challenged by Jephthah (see on Judges 12:6).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 3. Crying. Heb. qara’, not weeping, but calling on God for help.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Dried. From excessive speaking (see on Ps. 22:15).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 4. Hate me without a cause. Jesus applied this language to Himself (see John 15:25).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 5. My sins. Although the psalmist believes that he is suffering “without a cause” (v. 4) as far as the charges of his enemies are concerned, he nevertheless acknowledges that he is a sinner.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Are not hid. Compare Ps. 139:1–4.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
6. For my sake. That is, “on my account.” The psalmist pledges to do nothing that would make the faithful children of God ashamed. The principle here enunciated is an excellent motto for worthy Christian conduct. Let us never do anything that would bring dishonor upon the cause of God.
This verse is an excellent example of synonymous parallelism (see p. 24), the two halves having the same basic meaning.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 7. For thy sake. The real cause of the enmity was the psalmist’s devotion to God. Sinful men despise those who serve God (see MB 53). The conduct of the children of God
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Shame. Here referring to the slanderous charges heaped upon the psalmist (see Ps. 44:15, 16).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
8. My mother’s children. In an economy like that of the Hebrews, children of the same father were frequently only half brothers (see Ps. 50:20).
In the language of this verse, and of vs. 9, 20, Christ foretold, through David, the treatment that He was to receive from men (see AA 225).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 9. The zeal of thine house. The sanctuary is the object of the psalmist’s zeal. David showed his zeal in bringing the ark to Mt. Zion (see 2 Sam. 6:12–19); in desiring to build a permanent dwelling for the Lord in Jerusalem (see 2 Sam. 7:2); in collecting structural material for the building which he was not permitted to erect (see 1 Chron. 28:14–18; 29:2–5); and in instructing Solomon respecting the Temple (1 Chron. 28:9–13). When Jesus drove the money-changers and bargaining merchants from the Temple precincts, the disciples remembered that it was written of Him, “The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up” (see John 2:17; DA 158; see also AA 225). There is no place for a lackadaisical servant in the service of God.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
, “The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up” (see John 2:17; DA 158; see also AA 225). There is no place for a lackadaisical servant in the service of God.
The reproaches. Paul applied this sentence to Christ, who “pleased not himself” (see Rom. 15:3; cf. Ps. 89:50, 51; Jer. 20:8).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 10. With fasting. The psalmist endeavored to discipline himself through self-denial.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: To my reproach. The enemies mocked the psalmist because he was trying to be a sincere follower of God (see vs. 7–9).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 11. Sackcloth. An indication of repentance and humiliation (see on Ps. 30:11).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Proverb. Heb. mashal, “a proverbial saying,” or “a mocking saying”; rendered “by-word” in Ps. 44:14.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 12. They that sit. Either a reference to magistrates (see on Ruth 4:1), who would then be depicted as joining the rabble in ridiculing the psalmist, or an allusion to idlers loafing by the city gates (see on Ps. 9:14).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Speak against me. The psalmist is the subject of general conversation.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Drunkards. Literally, “drinkers of strong drink.” The psalmist is the subject of the satirical, ribald songs of intoxicated men (see Ps. 35:15, 16); he is the butt of their low jests (see Job 30:9).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 13. An acceptable time. Literally, “a time of favor” (see Isa. 49:8). The psalmist obviously felt that no time could be more acceptable than the present, when he was being unjustly reproached.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 14. Out of the mire. Compare v. 2.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 15. Pit. See on Ps. 28:1.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 16. Tender mercies. See on Ps. 51:1.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 17. Hide not thy face. See on Ps. 4:6; cf. Ps. 13:1; Ps. 30:7.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Hear me speedily. Literally, “answer me quickly.” The psalmist doubtless feels that he will perish if he does not have speedy relief.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 18. Draw nigh. The psalmist cannot endure forever the sense of distance between himself and God.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 19. Thou hast known. The psalmist finds consolation in his assurance that God knows (see Job 23:10).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 20. Reproach. Verses 20, 21 have Messianic application (see Matt. 27:34, 48; DA 746; AA 225; PK 691).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
To take pity. Compare Isa. 63:5. In Gethsemane the Saviour longed for sympathy in His suffering (see DA 687, 688). Later He was forsaken of all His disciples (see Matt. 26:56; Mark 14:50). The verse is an expression of supreme loneliness.
The two final clauses of the verse constitute a perfect synonymous parallelism, arranged in interlaced form:
             “And I look for some to take pity,
             but there was none;
             And for comforters,
             but I found none.”
The pathetic words of this verse are paraphrased in the recitative for tenor, “Thy Rebuke Hath Broken His Heart,” in Handel’s oratorio The Messiah.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 21. Gall. Heb. ro’sh, “poisonous herb,” translated “venom” in Deut. 32:33; “poison” in Job 20:16; and “hemlock” in Hosea 10:4. According to Mark 15:23 the “gall” offered to Jesus was myrrh.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Meat. Heb. baruth, “bread of consolation,” meaning the food supplied to a mourner by his symphatizers. The use of the word emphasizes the hypocrisy of their action.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Vinegar. For the Messianic fulfillment of the prophecy, see Matt. 27:34, 48; Mark 15:23; John 19:29, 30.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 22. Let their table. Verse 22 begins a series of imprecations continuing through v. 28 (on Imprecatory Psalms, see p. 624). Paul quotes vs. 22, 23 to describe the hardened sinners of his day (see Rom. 11:8–10).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 23. Be darkened. A figure denoting perplexity (see 2 Cor. 3:14).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 24. Pour out. See Ps. 79:6; Jer. 10:25.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 25. Habitation. Heb. tirah, “encampment,” or “enclosure,” like the circle of tents of a nomadic tribe, hence any place of abode, a camp, a castle, or a palace. The psalmist prays that the place of abode occupied by his enemies may be empty, and that they may perish. This verse is applied to the office held by Judas (see Acts 1:20).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 26. Talk to the grief. That is, they add to the sorrow of the afflicted by defaming his character and by misconstruing his expressions of impatience under trial (see on Ps. 41:5–8). This verse states an additional reason for the psalmist’s imprecation.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 27. Into thy righteousness. The psalmist prays that sinners may be treated as they deserve, not as if they were righteous.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 28. Blotted out. See on Ex. 32:32; cf. Ps. 56:8; Dan. 12:1; Phil. 4:3; Rev. 3:5; 13:8.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 29. But I. The psalmist uses the personal pronoun to introduce a sharp contrast between himself and the enemies mentioned in the preceding verses.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Poor. That is, “afflicted,” or “oppressed by misery.” As the psalmist prays for the enemies who are proud and lofty to be brought down, so he prays that he who is now in the depths of affliction may be “set … up on high.” Like Ps. 22 (see vs. 22–31), Ps. 69 closes with vows of gratitude and expressions of hopeful praise.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 30. Name. See on Ps. 5:11; 7:17.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: With a song. This psalm is a fulfillment of the psalmist’s vow of praise.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 31. Shall please. See on Ps. 40:6–8; 51:16, 17; 1 Sam. 15:22.

text: 5. Make haste unto me, O God. Instead of this clause, Ps. 40:17 has “The Lord thinketh upon me.” Also, instead of the Heb. ’Adonai, “Lord” (Ps. 40:17), Ps. 70:5 has ’Elohim, “God” (see on v. 1). For a discussion of the significance of the various divine names, see Vol. I, pp. 170–173.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: O Lord. Heb. Yahweh. Ps. 40:17 has ’Elohim. The profession of confidence in God (vs. 1–4) is here changed to a cry of need, and the tone of the poem closes in a plaintive mood. text: 6. By thee have I been holden up. Literally, “Upon thee have I braced myself.” As a child leans all its weight upon its parent, so David found constant support in God (see Ps. 22:9, 10; Isa. 46:3, 4).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Old age. His review of his past leads David to look toward the future, especially to that time when old age, “last scene of all, that ends the strange eventful history,” comes upon him. In contemplating the vicissitudes of old age, he feels the need of special grace (see 1T 422–424).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Strength faileth. If God was David’s “rock” and “fortress” when the psalmist was in the full strength of manhood, God would need to be a greater support when the psalmist faced old age with its physical and mental infirmities. On the glory of old age, see Prov. 16:31.

text: 1. Give the king. The psalm opens with a prayer for an ideal king. Solomon’s reign would have been a “reign of righteousness” like the one described in this psalm, if he had followed the divinely inspired counsel of his father (see PK 26; cf. superscription to Ps. 72).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Thy judgments. The ideal king will make his decisions according to God’s will (see on Deut. 1:17).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 2. He shall judge. Or, “may he judge.” This verb and the main verbs throughout the psalm may be translated as futures, describing the ideal king, as he shall be; or as optatives, expressing a wish, “may he judge,” etc. (see 1 Kings 3:6–9; Isa. 11:2–5; 32:1).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Thy poor. Righteous judgment of the poor, who are often the victims of unjust judgment, implies the impartial administration of justice (see on Deut. 1:17).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 3. Peace. Peace will reign in the land as the effect of righteousness (see Isa. 32:15–17). Peace brings material blessings to a country, whereas war spreads desolation. Messiah, the King of righteousness, was to be a King of peace (see Isa. 9:5, 6; 11:9; Zech. 9:10; cf. Heb. 7:2).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 4. He shall judge. See on v. 2. Verses 4–8 will have their complete fulfillment in the King of kings (see PP 755).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 6. Like rain. The rule of the ideal king, or King Messiah, is like the gentle showers, which make the mown grass spring up again fresh and beautiful (see 2 Sam. 23:3, 4; cf. Deut. 32:2; Isa. 55:10, 11; SC 72; MB 18).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 7. Flourish. Literally, “sprout,” “bud forth,” carrying on the figure of v. 6 (see Ps. 92:13).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 8. From sea to sea. See Gen. 15:18; see on Ex. 23:31; cf. Num. 34:3, 6; Ps. 89:25; Zech. 9:10; DA 458.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 9. Lick the dust. A figure describing prostration with heads touching the ground, an Oriental symbol of complete submission (see Isa. 49:23). Assyrian bas-reliefs show captives crouching, faces on the ground, groveling at the feet of their conquerors.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 10. Tarshish. See on Ps. 48:7.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 20. Prayers of David. This verse is probably an inscription of identification (a colophon), at the close of Book Two, to designate the fact that there are more Davidic psalms in Books One and Two than in Book Three (which carries the name of David in only one superscription). However, it has been observed that the verse may be interpreted as pertaining only to Ps. 72 in the sense that David had nothing more to pray for in that connection at that time.

text: 1. Truly. Heb. ’ak (see on Ps. 62:1). ’Ak appears also in v. 13 (translated “verily”), and in v. 18 (translated “surely”).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
God is good. Despite appearances to the contrary.
  “Yet, in the maddening maze of things, And tossed by storm and flood, To one fixed trust my spirit clings; I know that God is good!”
  WHITTIER, The Eternal Goodness.
This is the conclusion to which the psalmist has come, after a period of great perplexity. The psalm explains how he reached this conclusion.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Of a clean heart. Or, “of a pure heart” (see Ps. 24:4; 51:10; 73:13; Matt. 5:8).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 2. But as for me. The phrase concentrates our attention upon the psalmist and the experiences through which he passed in arriving at the solution of the problem of the psalm: Why do bad men prosper, and good men suffer?
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Were almost gone. A striking metaphor, meaning that the psalmist had almost lost his faith (see Ps. 44:18).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Well nigh slipped. See Ps. 17:5. The psalmist had been on the verge of slipping from the rock of faith into the pit of skepticism.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 3. Envious. See on Ps. 37:1. Such envy reveals a spirit that attaches more importance to the things of this world than to the favor of God.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Prosperity. Literally, “peace.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 4. Bands. Or “pangs.” To the psalmist it seemed that the wicked do not suffer the pangs of death, but that they come to a peaceful end (see Job 21:13, 23).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
4. Bands. Or “pangs.” To the psalmist it seemed that the wicked do not suffer the pangs of death, but that they come to a peaceful end (see Job 21:13, 23).
Firm. Better, “fat.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 5. Trouble. They seem to escape what is recognized as the common lot of men (see Job 5:7).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: As other men. From the Heb. ’enosh, “man in his frailty” (see on Ps. 8:4).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Like other men. From the Heb. ’adam, “mankind” (see on Ps. 8:4).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 6. Chain. Better, “necklace,” as adornment (see Prov. 1:9; 3:22).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: As a garment. Violence (see Gen. 6:11) is as habitual with them as their clothing (see Ps. 109:18, 19).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 7. Fatness. Not weakened by toil, as other men are are, they grow fat from high living.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: They have. They have whatever they wish. They have only to wish for something, and that wish is gratified; gratification surpasses expectation.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 8. Oppression. This verse may be translated, “They are corrupt, and speak wickedly; concerning oppression they speak loftily.” What a picture of the lofty air assumed by the wicked!
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
8. Oppression. This verse may be translated, “They are corrupt, and speak wickedly; concerning oppression they speak loftily.” What a picture of the lofty air assumed by the wicked!
9. Against the heavens. Or, “in the heavens,” by which may be meant, “They talk as if they were in the heavens.” The phrase is balanced with “through the earth” (literally, “in the earth”) in the second clause of the synonymous parallelism. They talk with an assumed authority. They keep busy going everywhere speaking “wickedly” (v. 8).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 10. His people. The exact meaning of this verse is not clear. The LXX gives a different reading: “Therefore my people shall return hither, and full days shall be found for them.” The RSV obtains its reading by a change of the Hebrew text. The Hebrew as it stands has been variously interpreted, some taking the pronoun “his” to refer to God, others to the wicked man. If the righteous are the subject of the verse, “return hither” may refer to a return to the problem highlighted in the psalm; if the wicked are the subject, the phrase describes the wicked returning to consort with their wicked leader.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

cked man. If the righteous are the subject of the verse, “return hither” may refer to a return to the problem highlighted in the psalm; if the wicked are the subject, the phrase describes the wicked returning to consort with their wicked leader.
11. How doth God know? See Ps. 10:4, 11, 13; 14:1.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 12. Who prosper. Compare Job 21:7–15.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 13. Verily. Heb. ’ak (see on v. 1).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: In vain. In view of the psalmist’s observations (vs. 3–12), he feels that there is no advantage in his being pure before God (see Job 9:27–31).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Washed my hands. Symbolic of innocence or purity (see Job 9:30).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 14. Plagued. The psalmist had previously claimed that the wicked are not “plagued” (v. 5).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Every morning. The psalmist’s reproof came with the return of every new day (see Job 7:18).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 15. If I say. Rather, “if I had said,” perhaps, to himself. Here begins the triumph of faith.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: I will speak thus. If I should express all that I think.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: I should offend. I should have hurt them, should have been untrue to them, should have put a stumbling block in their way. Therefore, the psalmist preferred to remain silent. Sublime reticence (see James 3:2)!
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 16. Too painful. The psalmist pondered the problem, seeking to explain the apparent injustice in God’s government, but the end result was only perplexity; the problem was too deep for him to solve.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 17. Until. The problem is about to find solution.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: The sanctuary. The psalmist ceased his endeavors to reason his way through to a solution of the problem, and went into the sanctuary (see 2 Kings 19:14). The real problems of life are solved only in communion with God.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Understood I. In the quietness of the sanctuary the psalmist’s doubts melted away. God gave him the real solution to the problem. Among other things, he learned that he had lost in his perspective and had exaggerated the prosperity of the wicked.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Their end. However prosperous the wicked may appear may appear to be, their position is precarious. They have no sure foothold, and may go down at any moment. The argument is even more forceful when applied to the ultimate annihilation of the wicked (Rev. 20:9, 14, 15).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 18. Destruction. That which restores the psalmist’s faith is his recognition of the end of the wicked in this world, of their downfall in the midst of their prosperity. Loss of perspective had kept the psalmist from seeing the retribution that often came upon the wicked, until he went into the sanctuary and cast himself wholly upon God. He had forgotten that Sodom and Gomorrah were destroyed by fire from heaven; that Pharaoh’s land was ruined by the plagues and his armies were drowned in the sea.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 19. As in a moment. The prosperity of wicked men, or of wicked governments, often collapses in a moment. The problem set forth in the psalm is solved only in a view of the end of the wicked, which may come at any moment.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: With terrors. Calamities that bring them terror (see Job 18:11; 24:17; 27:20).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 20. As a dream. Prosperity is like a dream (see Isa. 29:7, 8); reality returns when the sleeper awakes.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Their image. In the calm of eternity God will pay no attention to the dreams of human existence on earth; eternity will deal with those elements that constitute the real character of man.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 21. Thus. Or, “for.” The reason for his failure to find the solution to the problem lay in the fact that he was unable to consider the matter calmly. He “was grieved,” literally, “was soured,” the Hebrew word being used of leavening (see Ex. 12:34, 39). His heart had lost its sweetness, as if under the action of a ferment. Depressed spirits impair man’s judgment. The psalmist frankly acknowledges his error in endeavoring to solve the problem in an embittered state of mind, according to appearances, and not according to eternal values.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Reins. See on Ps. 7:9.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 22. Fool
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: I. The Hebrew pronoun has the emphatic initial position in the verse.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Before thee. The psalmist’s folly would have been bad enough had he been alone, but it was utterly reprehensible under the eye of God (see Ps. 51:4).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
23. I. The emphatic initial position as in v. 22. Although I complain and doubt God’s justice, yet God is with me; He will not drive me from His presence.
In vs. 23–28 the psalmist express the final solution to the problem of the psalm. That solution is in God, and in the consciousness of His presence and His guidance in this life and in the life everlasting. It is scarcely possible to express to express the sublime beauty of this exquisite passage, both in thought and in diction.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: My right hand. Compare Ps. 18:35; 63:8.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 24. With thy counsel. The psalmist recognizes God’s guidance, according to the divine plan for his life in this present world. Because he had failed to look to God for guidance and counsel, he had almost succumbed to doubt (see Ps. 48:14).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Afterward. When this life is finished.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: To glory. The poet here suggests his confidence in a future life. In the glory of heaven there will be no room for doubt. The glory, the true splendor, of the eternal life is contrasted with the “image,” the “dream,” the “vain show,” of the wicked man’s existence.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 25. In heaven. There is no one in heaven who can be compared with God. No one “can be to me what God is” (Barnes).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: None upon earth.. God is all-sufficient. All my happiness centers in Him. This intimacy of devotion is one of the cardinal teachings of the book of Psalms (see Ps. 42:1, 2; 63:1).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
None upon earth.. God is all-sufficient. All my happiness centers in Him. This intimacy of devotion is one of the cardinal teachings of the book of Psalms (see Ps. 42:1, 2; 63:1).
26. Strength. Literally, “rock.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Portion. Not friends, or honor, or wealth, or any earthly thing, but God was the source of the psalmist’s happiness. God was his all in all. Prompted by this verse, Charles Wesley (1707–88), on his deathbed, dictated to his wife one of his 6,500 hymns, in which appear the words: “Jesus, … strength of my failing flesh and heart.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 27. Far from thee. To be with God is life; to be far from Him is death. The psalmist’s realization of this fact solved the problem of God’s dealings with men (see vs. 3–12).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Go a whoring. God’s relation to His people is frequently compared to that of marriage (see Ps. 45; Jer. 3:8, 9, 14; 5:7; 13:27; 2 Cor. 11:2; Eph. 5:25; James 4:4). When God’s children are estranged from Him, they are unfaithful to their marriage vows. The phrase “a whoring” consists of the preposition “a” and the verbal noun “whoring.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 28. Draw near to God See Heb. 10:22. When we draw nigh to God He draws nigh to us (see James 4:8). There is a beautiful reciprocal relationship between man and God: the closer we draw to Him, the more fully He is able to reveal Himself.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Lord God. The Hebrew reads ’Adonai Yahweh, an unusual combination (see Vol. I, pp. 171–173). Beneath the psalmist’s doubts, there had always been a measure of trust in God. Henceforth there should be no more doubt, only serene trust.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: That I may declare. The psalmist recognizes his responsibility to tell others how he has passed from doubt to confidence, how he has solved in the Lord Jehovah the problem that is the theme of the psalm. The psalm closes with this solemn vow.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 1. Cast us off. See Ps. 13:1; 43:2; 44:9; 79:5. It seems that God has disowned His people (see Lam. 5:20).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Smoke. Smoke suggests fire; anger is frequently compared to fire (see Deut. 32:22; Ps. 18:7, 8; cf. Lam. 2:3).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Sheep of thy pasture.. Compare Ps. 79:13; 95:7. In calling the people God’s sheep, the psalmist heightens the tenderness of his appeal. How strange, he implies, that God should cast off His defenseless people, who are most in need of His care.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
Sheep of thy pasture.. Compare Ps. 79:13; 95:7. In calling the people God’s sheep, the psalmist heightens the tenderness of his appeal. How strange, he implies, that God should cast off His defenseless people, who are most in need of His care.
2. Thou hast purchased. See Ex. 15:16.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: The rod. Heb. shebeṭ, “staff.” The “staff” came to denote the tribe, probably from its use as a symbol of authority, religious or secular.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Inheritance. See Ps. 28:9; cf. Deut. 32:8. Israel is called the “rod of thine inheritance” (see Jer. 10:16).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Thou hast redeemed. See the phraseology of Ex. 15:13.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Mount Zion. See on Ps. 48:2.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 3. Lift up thy feet. The psalmist beseeches God to come quickly to visit the ruins of Mt. Zion and to intervene.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Perpetual desolations. Ruins so extensive as to appear complete and permanent. It seemed that they would never be built again.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Hath done. The Babylonians had carried off everything that was valuable (see 2 Kings 25:13–17), and had set fire to the Temple (see Ps. 74:7). A description of the desecration follows in vs. 4–8. These details tend to establish the historical background of the psalm, as given in the Introduction.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 4. Roar. The reference is to the tumult of war, the invading despoilers being likened to wild beasts (see Isa. 5:29; Jer. 2:15).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Ensigns. They impudently set up their battle standards in place of the true emblems of Jehovah. The holy place fell under the sway of a foreign power (see Num. 2:2). Pagan standards set up in the Temple marked the height of ignominy for the Jews.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 5. Lifted up axes. The enemy-soldiers are pictured as chopping up the woodwork of the Temple.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 6. But. Or, “and.” The activities of vs. 5, 6 are continuous and contemporary, not contrasting.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Carved work. See 1 Kings 6:29. This was cut down, broken off, probably for the sake of the gold overlay (see 1 Kings 6:22, 32, 35).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 7. Have cast fire. The Babylonians actually set fire to the Temple (see 2 Kings 25:9).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Dwelling place. See Ex. 20:24; Deut. 12:11.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: To the ground. The Temple was polluted by being made a heap of ruins (see Lam. 2:2).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 8. Synagogues. Literally, “places of meeting.” The translation “synagogue” occurs here doubtless because it was not known that the synagogue was a late (postexilic) institution. The Jewish word for synagogue is beth hakkeneseth.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
8. Synagogues. Literally, “places of meeting.” The translation “synagogue” occurs here doubtless because it was not known that the synagogue was a late (postexilic) institution. The Jewish word for synagogue is beth hakkeneseth.
9. Our signs. See v. 4.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Any prophet. Compare Lam. 2:9; Eze. 7:26.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: How long. This verse presents Israel’s cup of misery as filled; it is the saddest verse in the psalm.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 10. Blaspheme thy name. Compare a similar appeal in vs. 18, 22. It seems that calamities will never cease. This appeal to the honor of God is frequent in the OT (see Ex. 32:12, 13; Num. 14:13–16; Deut. 9:28).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 11. Out of thy bosom. Why does not God stretch forth His hand to deliver Israel? He appears to keep His hand in the folds of His robe. The psalmist expresses impatience because he thinks that God should demonstrate His power by annihilating the invaders.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
hand in the folds of His robe. The psalmist expresses impatience because he thinks that God should demonstrate His power by annihilating the invaders.
12. For. The psalmist takes comfort in contemplating God’s previous deliverances of His people. Recounting the past gives comfort for the present and hope for the future (see LS 196).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: My King. See Ps. 44:4. The poet is sure that, despite appearances, God still rules.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Salvation. Literally, “salvations,” that is, “divine acts of salvation.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Midst of the earth. Compare Ex. 8:22.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 13. Thou. In the Hebrew the pronoun is in the emphatic initial position here and in vs. 14, 15, 17 (see Ps. 65:9–11).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Didst divide the sea. At the time of the crossing of the Red Sea (see Ex. 14:21; cf. Ps. 77:16).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Dragons. Heb. tanninim, “see monsters,” presumably symbolic of Egyptian power (see Eze. 29:3). The allusion seems to be to the destruction of Pharaoh’s armies in the Red Sea (see Ex. 14:27–30; 15:4).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 14. Heads of leviathan. See on Isa. 27:1. Evidently another allusion to Egypt’s power (see on v. 13).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: People inhabiting. The wild creatures of the desert (see Prov. 30:25, 26). The literal language portrays the monsters of the deep killed, thrown upon the shore, and made food for the wild creatures.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 15. Thou didst cleave. The allusion may be to God’s bringing water out of the rock at the command of Moses (see Ex. 17:6; Num. 20:8; cf. Ps. 78:15, 16), or to the passage of the Red Sea (see Joshua 2:10), or to the crossing of the Jordan (see Joshua 3:13; 4:23; 5:1).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Driedst up mighty rivers. An obvious allusion to the crossing of the Jordan (see Joshua 3:13; 4:23; 5:1).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 16. Thine. The poet’s view enlarges from God’s miracles in delivering His people, to the wider view of God’s constant power and glory in nature.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Light. Heb. ma’or, “luminary,” here probably the sun (see Gen. 1:15, 16; cf. Ps. 136:7–9).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 17. Borders. Natural land and sea boundaries (see Gen. 1:9; Job 26:10; Jer. 5:22).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 18. Remember. Compare v. 2.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Hath reproached. See Lam. 1:7; 2:7, 15, 16; see on Ps. 74:10; cf. v. 22.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Name. See on Ps. 5:11; 7:17.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 19. Turtledove. God’s children are exquisitely compared to a tender and gentle dove, beloved of God.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 22. Plead. The psalmist realizes that the cause is God’s, and that it is God’s honor that is concerned. Whatever is done to God’s children is regarded as done to Him. It is well for puny man to recognize God’s ultimate concern and adjust himself as an instrument in God’s hands to work out the will of God.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 23. Forget not. The psalmist closes his prayer with a petition for just retribution upon the enemies (cf. 2 Kings 19:28).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Tumult. The reference is evidently to the enemies invading Jerusalem with loud war cries.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

verse_ref: Those That Rise Up Against Thee
text: Those that rise up against thee. Those who set themselves in opposition to God’s purposes by working against His appointed leaders often deceive themselves into believing that their course of action is of no particular concern to God (see Ex. 16:8; 1 Sam. 8:7).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
Increaseath. Rather, “ascends.”
The psalm seems to break off almost abruptly, as if the psalmist were stopped in the midst of his portrayal of the increasing depredations in the land.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 1. Do we give thanks. The use of the first person plural pronoun suggests that the psalm was intended for public worship. The repetition of the phrase lends liturgical emphasis.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
1. Do we give thanks. The use of the first person plural pronoun suggests that the psalm was intended for public worship. The repetition of the phrase lends liturgical emphasis.
Name. See on Ps. 5:11; 7:17.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Is near. In His manifestation of power in delivering Israel from the enemy, God manifests His nearness (see Deut. 4:7).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Thy wondrous works declare. Or, “they recount Thy wondrous deeds.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 2. Congregation. Heb. mo‘ed, “set time,” “assembly,” “place of assembly.” God is introduced as Speaker (see Ps. 46:10). He chooses the opportune time, the exact moment best suited to His purposes. In our human impatience, we tend to run ahead of God (see Hab. 2:3).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Uprightly. When God judges, there is equal justice for all (see 2 Sam. 23:3; Ps. 58:1).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 3. Are dissolved. When the land seems about to melt before the invader, God steps in to sustain. Without God, everything would fail.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Pillars. The earth is likened to a strong building upheld by pillars.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Selah. See p. 629.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 4. Horn. Frequently a symbo1 of strength (see 1 Sam. 2:10; Ps. 89:24).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 5. With a stiff neck. That is, arrogantly, imperiously, obstinately; the phrase “a stiff neck” is common in the Pentateuch (see Ex. 32:9; 33:3, 5; Deut. 9:6, 13; 31:27).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
5. With a stiff neck. That is, arrogantly, imperiously, obstinately; the phrase “a stiff neck” is common in the Pentateuch (see Ex. 32:9; 33:3, 5; Deut. 9:6, 13; 31:27).
6. Promotion. Literally, “lifting up.” Success does not come from natural geographic advantages or from nations inhabiting the regions at the four points of the compass, but from man’s conformity to God’s eternal plan (see MH 476, 477). The ultimate issue is decided by God (see v. 7).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Putteth down. True of individuals and of nations (see 1 Sam. 2:7, 8; Ps. 147:6; Dan. 2:21; 4:17).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 8. Cup. God is represented as holding in His hand a cup for men to drink (see on Ps. 60:3; cf. Isa. 51:17, 22; Rev. 14:9, 10).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Full of mixture. Mixed with spices, to make the wine stronger and increase its intoxicating power (see Prov. 9:2; 23:30; Isa. 5:22).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Dregs. The wicked must empty the cup, drinking its entire contents. This impressive picture of the righteous judgment of God is well calculated to inspire a fear of sin.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 9. I. The psalmist speaks for himself, and, as an act of public worship, for the people of Israel.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Will declare. The psalmist pledges himself to declare the righteousness of God’s dealing with men (see v. 1).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 10. Horns. See on v. 4.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
Will I cut off. “I” may mean God; the Hebrew language abounds in such sudden changes in person. The psalmist may speak for God, or the psalmist may speak for the people, confident that God will assist them in defeating the wicked.
The psalm closes with a universal statement of God’s just government.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
ELLEN G. WHITE COMMENTS
  6, 7 MH 476
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 1. Is God known. See Ps. 9:16; 48:3.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Name. See on Ps. 5:11; 17:7.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
Israel. The synonymous parallelism of the two clauses of this verse indicates that “Israel” is synonymous with “Judah.” The names evidently do not here refer to the two divisions of the nation, which divisions most likely were effected after the time the psalm was composed (see GC 23).
In v. 1–3 Jerusalem is celebrated as the abode of God, whence He displays His power.
76
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 2. Salem. The shorter and older name for Jerusalem; the “peaceful” place, where God’s presence abode (see on Gen. 14:18; see also PP 703).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Zion. See on Ps. 48:2.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 3. There. In Zion, whence God’s power was displayed.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Arrows of the bow. Literally, “flames of the bow,” probably describing arrows flying with the speed of lightning.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Battle. The idea is that the enemies’ devices were completely upset by the power of God (see Ps. 46:9).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Selah. See p. 629.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 4. More glorious. Verses 4–6 describe the sudden destruction of the invaders.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Mountains of prey. Perhaps thus designated because they are considered as the stronghold of robbers, from which these bandits went forth to plunder. God, who made the mountains, is superior to them in power and glory. The LXX reads, “everlasting mountains.”
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 5. The stouthearted. The invaders, boasting of their strength.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Have slept their sleep. They are dead (see on Ps. 13:3).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Found their hands. The mighty men are paralyzed, unable to use their hands to resist.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 6. At thy rebuke. When God spoke, they were discomfited.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: The chariot and horse. Charioteers and horsemen (by the figure of metonymy; cf. Isa. 43:17).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 7. Thou, even thou. Emphatic repetition. Verses 7–9 describe the destruction of the enemy as an act of judgment that teaches a lesson to all the world.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Art to be feared. Or, “art to be reverenced,” because His power has overthrown the enemy.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: When once. Better, “from the time.” If such invading armies have been overcome by God’s sudden display of power, who could possibly resist God with any hope of success?
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 8. Judgment. The overthrow of the enemy was regarded as a judgment from heaven.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Was still. The earth appeared to be silent, reverently listening to the voice of God pronouncing judgment (see Ps. 114:3–7).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 9. When God arose. See Ps. 3:7; 7:6; 44:26; 68:1.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 10. Shall praise thee. The wickedness of man gives occasion for great deeds on God’s part. Man’s hostility to God gives opportunity for the display of God’s power that brings praise to Him (see Ex. 9:16; 18:11).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Restrain. Literally, “thou wilt gird.” The parallelism of the two clauses in the verse indicates that God puts on, as an ornament, the last powerless efforts of feeble man to assert his own strength, clothing Himself thus to His own glory. The experience of Daniel is a notable example of the operation of this principle (see PK 543, 544).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 11. Vow. The poet addresses God’s people (see Ps. 22:25).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Bring presents. Our measure of gratitude is sometimes shown in our gifts.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 12. He shall cut off. God will cut down their pride, referring to what He had done as celebrated in this psalm. “Cut off” suggests the work of a vinedresser, pruning the vines or cutting off the clusters of grapes (see Isa. 18:5).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Spirit. Heb. ruach, literally, “wind” (see on Eccl. 12:7).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Kings. God defeats the plans of kings as well as of princes when His good pleasure dictates. The psalm closes with an expression of the finality of God’s dealing with evil men. Compare Rev. 6:15–17; 19:17–21.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
ELLEN G. WHITE COMMENTS
  1–12 PK 362
  2 GC 23
  10 PK 543; 5T 453
  11 4T 471
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 1. I cried. Verses 1–6 show the intensity of the psalmist’s feelings. There is a fluctuation between statement of fact and expression of desire and emotion.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 2. In the day. See Ps. 50:15; cf. 35:3. Ps. 77:2, 3 shows the reality and intensity of the prayer. Everything the psalmist did, even meditating on God, seemed but to intensify his grief.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: My sore. Literally, “my hand.” The interpretation “sore” comes from the idea that “hand” may be the symbol of a “stroke” (see Job 23:2, where “stroke” is literally “hand”). The translation “my hand is stretched out” (RSV) is apparently based on Jerome. The Hebrew verb translated “ran,” seems elsewhere always to have the meaning “run,” “flow,” “be poured” (see 2 Sam. 14:14).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
ranslation “my hand is stretched out” (RSV) is apparently based on Jerome. The Hebrew verb translated “ran,” seems elsewhere always to have the meaning “run,” “flow,” “be poured” (see 2 Sam. 14:14).
My soul. Or, “I” (see on Ps. 16:10).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Refused. Compare Gen. 37:35; Jer. 31:15. The experience of the psalmist should give comfort to those who fail to find an immediate answer to the honest questions of their soul.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 3. Was troubled. The more the psalmist meditated upon the incomprehensible administration of God’s government, the sadder he became, and the more inclined to rebel.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Overwhelmed. Compare Ps. 143:4, 5.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
Jacob and Joseph. Jacob is mentioned obviously because he was the father of the twelve tribes; Joseph, probably because he played so important a part in the affairs of Egypt.
Selah. See p. 629.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 4. Thou holdest mine eyes waking. Literally, “Thou holdest the watches of mine eyes.” God keeps him from sleeping, so that he worries all the night.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 5. Days of old. The psalmist reviews Israel’s history in an attempt to answer the questions of his heart (see LS 196; cf. vs. 14–20; see also Deut. 32:7; Isa. 63:11).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 6. Song. Heb. neginah, probably “music of stringed instruments.” The plural form of the word appears in the superscriptions to many of the psalms (for example Ps. 4; 55; 76).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: In the night. The psalmist shows a fondness for meditation and prayer in the stillness of the night (see Ps. 16:7; 17:3).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Commune. His communings are expressed in the form of questions (vs. 7–9).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 7. Cast off for ever. The questions uppermost in the psalmist’s mind were: Will God entirely forsake me? Will He abandon Israel?
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 8. Mercy. Or, “love,” Heb. chesed (see Additional Note on Ps. 36).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Promise. Evidently the promise to the patriarchs (see Gen. 17:7–13; 26:24; etc.).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: For evermore. Literally, “to generation and generation.” God’s love and His promise are the bulwarks of the psalmist’s faith as they can be of ours.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 9. Gracious. The psalmist seems to feel that God has abandoned one of the chief attributes of His character (see Ex. 34:6).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Tender mercies. See Ps. 25:6.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 10. My infirmity. The psalmist does not find fault with God, but recognizes his own inability to understand God’s ways, his own weakness of spirit.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Years. Heb. shenoth. The word may be interpreted as either “years” or “changing.” If it is interpreted as “years,” the sense of the verse appears to be: “This is my grief, that the very remembrance of God’s help in times past increases my sorrow and perplexity.” If the word is interpreted as “changing,” the sense appears to be: “It is my grief that the right hand of the Most High has changed” (RSV); in which case the psalmist is perplexed because he fails to see God dealing with him as He had dealt with him in times past.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 11. I will remember. Compare Ps. 143:5. Verse 11 marks the transition from the grief and expostulation of the first section of the poem to the hope and confidence of the second section.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
11. I will remember. Compare Ps. 143:5. Verse 11 marks the transition from the grief and expostulation of the first section of the poem to the hope and confidence of the second section.
13. In the sanctuary. Or, “in holiness.” God’s way, although men may not understand it, is always holy, just, and right (see Gen. 18:25). If the KVJ translation “in the sanctuary” is accepted, the verse may be interpreted to mean that God’s way is best understood in the place where He is worshiped, and from the principles expounded there (see PK 49, 50).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 14. Declared thy strength. As, for instance, in the Red Sea experience described in vs. 16–20.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: People. Literally, “peoples” (plural), the heathen nations that heard of the destruction of Pharaoh and the enemies of Egypt (see Ex. 15:14–16).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 15. Thine arm. The arm is the symbol of strength (see Ex. 6:6; 15:16; Ps. 10:15;98:1).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Redeemed. The miracle of Israel’s deliverance from Egypt is brought forth as a supreme example of God’s power to save and hence as a pledge of His continual power to save His people (see Ps. 78:12, 13; 106:21, 22; 114:1–5; etc.).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text:
Redeemed. The miracle of Israel’s deliverance from Egypt is brought forth as a supreme example of God’s power to save and hence as a pledge of His continual power to save His people (see Ps. 78:12, 13; 106:21, 22; 114:1–5; etc.).
Jacob and Joseph. Jacob is mentioned obviously because he was the father of the twelve tribes; Joseph, probably because he played so important a part in the affairs of Egypt.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 16. The waters
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Saw. The personification, in which the waters are represented as recognizing the presence of God and fleeing in fear, is eminently sublime. The waters fled to make way for God’s people.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: They were afraid. Literally, “they were in pain,” as of travail.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 17. Arrows. Lightning. Verses 17 and 18 describe the tempest, hurricane, thunder, lightning, accompanying the rolling back of the waters (see on Ps. 18:6–14; PP 287).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 18. Voice. See on Ps. 29:3.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Lightened the world. Compare Ps. 97:4.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 19. Thy way. Though invisible, God was with His people as they went through the dry bed of the sea (see Ex. 15:13; Ps. 78:52, 53). God is always with His children when they follow His guidance.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: 20. Like a flock. In sharp contrast to the majesty and power of God portrayed in the preceding verses, the psalmist now presents the tenderness of the Good Shepherd (see Ps. 78:52; Isa. 63:11 see DA 480).
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III

text: Moses and Aaron. God was the real Leader; Moses and Aaron were His instruments (see Num. 33:1). As God delivered Israel at the Red Sea, so He will deliver His people in time of peril. This realization should help us to put our trust in Him at all times. The psalm closes with assurance in the redemptive power of God.
author: Comentário Bíblico Adventista III
